hints: Notice that both equilibria share the same ion, $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})$, so they must compete with each other for it.
Adding $\text{NH}_3$ uses up $\text{Ag}^+$ to make the complex ion $\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2^+$, which lowers free $[\text{Ag}^+]$.
Apply Le Chatelier to equilibrium 1 and ask which way it must shift to replace the $\text{Ag}^+$ that has been removed.
walkthrough:
**Picture the two competing equilibria**

Think of $\text{Ag}^+$ as being pulled in two directions. It can join $\text{X}^-$ to form solid $\text{AgX}$, or it can join $\text{NH}_3$ to form the soluble complex.

$$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{X}^-(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{AgX}(\text{s})$$
$$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{NH}_3(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2^+(\text{aq})$$

**Recall how insoluble the silver halides are**

Silver halides are very insoluble, especially $\text{AgI}$. That means equilibrium 1 lies far to the right, with almost all $\text{Ag}^+$ precipitated.

Solubility order is $\text{AgCl} > \text{AgBr} > \text{AgI}$, so $\text{AgI}$ is the hardest to redissolve.

**Couple the equilibria with Le Chatelier**

When you add $\text{NH}_3$, equilibrium 2 moves to the right to make more complex. This removes free $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq})$ from solution.

Equilibrium 1 then has to oppose this change. It moves to the left, so solid $\text{AgX}$ dissolves to release more $\text{Ag}^+$. This is why $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute ammonia but $\text{AgI}$ does not.

options.A: Incorrect. For $\text{X}^- = \text{I}^-$, $\text{AgI}$ is extremely insoluble with a very small $K_{sp}$. Equilibrium 1 lies far to the right, not to the left. That is why $\text{AgI}$ precipitate does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia.
options.B: Correct. More $\text{NH}_3$ drives equilibrium 2 to the right, forming $\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2^+$. This lowers $[\text{Ag}^+]$, so by Le Chatelier equilibrium 1 shifts left to dissolve some $\text{AgX}(\text{s})$ and replace $\text{Ag}^+$.
options.C: Incorrect. The $K_c$ expression for equilibrium 2 only involves $\text{Ag}^+$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2^+$. It does not contain $\text{X}^-$, so its value is independent of whether $\text{Cl}^-$ or $\text{I}^-$ was originally present.
options.D: Incorrect. Check oxidation numbers. In equilibrium 2, Ag stays as +1, N stays as -3 in $\text{NH}_3$, and H stays as +1. No electron transfer occurs, so it is a complex formation (ligand substitution) reaction, not redox.
